final.title: Design scope creep out before the build starts
final.body:
Scope creep usually starts when a small business treats “maybe later” as part of the current build.

If you are considering workflow automation, keep the boundary simple: one recurring workflow, one owner-controlled measure, one fixed pilot scope. That is not a limitation of the work. It is the thing that keeps the conversation inspectable.

A useful diagnostic question is: what is the one repeatable workflow that costs time or creates risk, and how will you know if it is working? If the answer starts branching into invoices, customer support, lead follow-up, and reporting all at once, the scope is already slipping.

Bareni’s normal sequence is simple: a free 30-minute diagnostic, then a one-page pilot proposal with scope, price, and measures, then a paid MVP or pilot inside a defined boundary. The timings are intended scopes, not guarantees. If a new request appears mid-build, the right move is to say, “That is a separate workflow,” and decide whether it belongs in a later pilot. Dry, but useful.

For a practical next step, write down one weekly workflow that is easy to observe and has a clear success measure you choose yourself, such as customer questions answered within a set time or invoices logged within a set time. Bring that to the diagnostic. Human approval stays with you; the scope should too.

final.title: Design scope creep out before the build starts
final.body:
Scope creep is not really a build problem. It is a decision problem.

For a small business, the cleanest boundary is simple: pick one recurring workflow, define the measure, and write the scope before any build starts. In the Bareni diagnostic, that means asking: what is the one repeatable workflow that costs time or creates risk, and how will we know it is better?

That question matters because it keeps the work inspectable. If the current workflow is invoice logging, then the pilot is about invoice logging. If someone wants customer replies, lead follow-up, and reporting in the same pass, that is not one workflow. It is three.

The practical control is to write a short scope check in advance. One workflow. One owner. One measurable outcome. One approval boundary. If a new request appears during the build, pause and decide whether it belongs in this pilot or the next one.

That is not being difficult. It is how you keep a small automation investment from turning into a loose pile of “while you’re in there” requests.

The next step is to name one weekly workflow, in plain English, and write down the success measure you already use today. That becomes the input for the diagnostic and the proposal.
